project.name: RogueLike
project.description: Turn-based roguelike dungeon crawler built on Godot 4.6 / C# (.NET 8). Layered DDD architecture: pure C# Godot-free Domain holds all game rules (grid, BSP generation, FOV, turn loop, actors/AI, combat, items, progression) and is unit-tested in isolation; thin Godot Node2D View controllers render and delegate downward.

nodes.name: CLAUDE.md
nodes.summary: Authoritative architecture and workflow ledger for the project, documenting the three-project layered DDD layout (Godot-free Domain + thin Godot View controllers), build/test commands, rich-domain modelling rules, and C#/Godot coding standards.
nodes.languageNotes: Serves as the canonical Claude Code instruction file; encodes the Godot-free Domain wall, TDD/small-batch workflow, and member-ordering/var/collection-expression style gates.

nodes.name: REFACTORING_OPPORTUNITIES.md

nodes.languageNotes: EnforceCodeStyleInBuild makes collection-expression/var style violations fail the build; Compile Remove globs carve out Domain and both test projects so the game project carries no test packages.

nodes.name: RogueLike.sln
nodes.summary: Visual Studio solution tying together the four projects across two solution folders: Domain { RogueLike.Domain, RogueLike.Domain.Tests } and View { RogueLike, RogueLike.View.Tests }.
nodes.languageNotes: NestedProjects section groups each layer with its test project; the View game project carries ExportDebug/ExportRelease configs for Godot export, which the Domain/test projects do not.

tour.title: The Architecture Contract
tour.description: Start here: CLAUDE.md is the authoritative ledger that explains the project's single most important idea. RogueLike is a turn-based Godot/C# roguelike built as a teaching example of rich-domain DDD layering: pure C# game rules (Code/Domain, completely Godot-free) hold all logic and are unit-tested in isolation, while thin Godot Node controllers (Code/View) only render and forward input. SYSTEM_DESIGN.md is the companion ledger that catalogs every core system and tracks the anemic-to-rich migration status; read both before touching code.

tour.title: Project Layout & Build
tour.description: Before reading code, see how the contract from Step 1 is enforced structurally. RogueLike.sln ties together four projects in two solution folders, and the two .csproj files draw the Godot-free wall: the Domain library uses a plain Microsoft.NET.Sdk with no Godot reference, while the game project uses Godot.NET.Sdk and references Domain one-way. This compile-time separation is what makes the 'rules can't depend on Godot' rule physically impossible to violate.

tour.title: The Value Object Vocabulary
tour.description: Every layer builds on these immutable value objects, and GridPos is the single most depended-upon type in the whole codebase (highest fan-in). GridPos is a grid coordinate with Manhattan/Chebyshev distance and Step helpers; Direction is the eight-way movement type with delta vectors and a FromDelta factory. Crucially, the domain never uses Godot's Vector2I — it speaks only in these VOs, which is what keeps the domain Godot-free.
tour.languageLesson: These are immutable C# value objects: no setters, equality-by-value, and operations like Step return a new instance rather than mutating. The self-validating constructor makes invalid states unconstructable — a core DDD building block.

tour.title: The Dungeon Grid
tour.description: DungeonGrid is the core walkability data structure: it stores CellType per cell and answers bounds, walkability, line-of-sight, and step queries. Building on the GridPos vocabulary from Step 3, note the deliberate boundary — the grid holds NO map-generation logic. Pathfinding lives in a separate partial file that adds A* FindPath over walkable eight-way neighbors, keeping the data structure focused.
tour.languageLesson: C# partial classes split one class across files. Here DungeonGrid.cs holds the data/queries and DungeonGrid.Pathfinding.cs adds the A* algorithm — same class, separated concerns, both compiled together.

tour.title: Building the Map: BSP Generation
tour.description: Per the architecture rule, map generation must NEVER live in DungeonGrid — it lives in standalone builders. BspDungeonGenerator partitions space into a BspNode tree, carves rooms into a fresh DungeonGrid, and connects them with tunnels. This is a clean example of a pure algorithm (high fan-out, consuming GridPos and GridRect) that operates on the grid without being part of it.

tour.title: Field of View & Fog of War
tour.description: Field-of-view is modeled as a strategy pattern. IFovAlgorithm declares ComputeFov over a FovMap and DungeonGrid; Raycaster implements it by casting Bresenham rays in a 360-degree circle, stopping at walls. FovMap stores per-cell VisibilityState (unseen/explored/visible) and resets the visible layer each pass — this is what drives the fog of war the player sees.
tour.languageLesson: IFovAlgorithm is an interface (strategy pattern): Raycaster is one implementation, but callers depend on the abstraction, so a different FOV algorithm could be swapped in without changing the consumers.

tour.title: The Turn Loop
tour.description: Roguelikes are turn-based, and TurnManager is the heartbeat: a Player-to-Enemy state machine whose EndPlayerTurn/EndEnemyTurn methods advance CurrentState (a TurnState enum) and raise OnTurnChanged. The event-based design means the view reacts to turn changes without the domain knowing anything about Godot — the recurring decoupling pattern across this codebase.

tour.title: Actors, Movement & AI
tour.description: Actors live on the grid through pure-C# rules. IActor exposes a GridPosition and whether it's the player; ActorRegistry keys all actors by GridPos and guards single-tile occupancy; GridMover validates each step against terrain and occupancy. On top of these, EnemyAI is a melee decision tree (chase a visible player, attack when adjacent) and ArcherAI adds ranged logic (shoot on clear line of sight and range, otherwise chase). All of this is testable with zero Godot.

tour.title: Rich Combat: Behavior With Data
tour.description: Combat is the clearest illustration of the rich-domain principle. Health is an immutable VO whose TakeDamage/Heal/WithIncreasedMax return new clamped instances; Damage self-validates against negatives. ICombatant doesn't hand state to an external service — its default-implemented TryAttack produces Damage, applies it, logs to the GameLog, and triggers OnKilled. The verb lives on the entity that owns the data, not in a static *System mutator.
tour.languageLesson: C# default interface methods let ICombatant ship a complete TryAttack implementation in the interface itself, so every combatant shares the same attack flow without inheriting from a base class.

tour.title: Items, Inventory & Progression
tour.description: This cluster of tightly coupled domain types models loot. IItem's default TryPickup checks eligibility, adds itself to an Inventory, logs, and runs OnPickup; FloorItems registers items on the floor and delegates to TryPickup on actor arrival; Inventory is a slot-limited aggregate that removes consumables on use. ExperienceSystem tracks XP and level-ups, and GameLog is the singleton message bus all of these broadcast through — the same event-driven decoupling as the turn loop.

tour.title: The View Wrapper: Thin Controllers
tour.description: Now cross the wall into Godot. ActorController is the abstract Node2D base that owns a Health VO and exposes damage/heal/die; PlayerController handles input, movement, attacks and item use; EnemyController and ArcherController wrap the domain EnemyAI/ArcherAI and just sync sprite position and FOV visibility. The lesson: these controllers contain no game rules — they render and delegate downward to the domain types from Steps 8-10.

tour.title: Orchestration & The Conversion Bridge
tour.description: Main.cs is the top-level orchestrator (highest fan-out in the View): it wires up the grid, registries, turn manager and FOV, generates a level via BSP, spawns entities via the Spawner, drives FOV recompute and enemy turns, and handles descent and restart-on-death. GridConversions is the single sanctioned bridge translating domain GridPos to Godot's Vector2I/Vector2 — Vector2I is confined to this view edge, which is exactly how the domain stays Godot-free.

tour.title: Scenes & Resources: The Runnable Game
tour.description: Code becomes a game through Godot scenes. project.godot declares Main.tscn as the main scene and defines the input action map; Main.tscn instances the Player, dungeon tilemap and HUD overlays under the Main orchestrator node; Player.tscn binds the PlayerController script, sprite and camera. LevelSettings is a Godot Resource exposing inspector-tunable spawn knobs that the Spawner reads per level.
tour.languageLesson: Godot .tscn scene files wire scripts and assets onto a node tree, and project.godot's main_scene setting is the runtime entry point. Scenes compose the game declaratively; scripts (the controllers) supply behavior.

tour.title: The Two-Tier Test Strategy
tour.description: The tour closes where the architecture pays off: testing. The Godot-free domain is covered by fast xUnit tests (Domain.Tests, runnable with plain dotnet test and no Godot) — DungeonGridPathfindingTest, TurnManagerTest, HealthTest and friends exercise pure rules in isolation. The thin view layer needs headless Godot, so GridConversionsTest runs under gdUnit4 via test.runsettings. This split — fast logic tests vs. slow integration tests — is the entire point of keeping rules out of the nodes.
